## Sentence Architecture

### Ask the Channel Before the Device

**Also called:** the rhythm selector, who sets the pace, channel before device
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `rhythm.` shelf. It does not describe a cadence. It asks the three questions the shelf's own pair graph asks over and over — **who sets the pace, what size of thing you are actually shaping, and whether the sentence answers to anything outside its own effect** — and hands back a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were not invented: they were read off the `Yields to:` conditions the cards carry, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card cited here is cited by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card never reaches the page or the microphone. It exists so the device that does reach them was chosen against the channel, the unit and the obligation, rather than reached for because it is the writer's favourite.
**Used for and where it works best:** Answer the three questions **in order and out loud, in one sentence each, before you open the shelf.** Question one eliminates most of the shelf only when the answer is not *the page*; question two is the one that always works, because every card on this shelf is about exactly one size of thing; question three is a gate rather than a sort — if the answer is yes, the shortlist collapses to the small block written for somebody else's constraint, and the rest of the shelf is not available to you at all. Where two answers fight for one piece — a script that is heard and also printed as captions — that is two passes, and the shelf says so in its own words: *two passes rather than one compromise* (`rhythm.vo_breath_line`).
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **You are diagnosing a fault rather than choosing a device.** The shelf's named failures are kept off this map on purpose, and a writer who arrives saying *my prose is flat* or *this splice is wrong* is not choosing — they are being sent, and the destination is already written on the failure card they came from. Also avoid it on anything **sung**: `lyric.` owns the shape of a sung line, and the one card here that touches metre is a border marker rather than an alternative to a lyric card. Also avoid reaching through it for **a rate**: `pacing.` owns words per minute for the whole package and `tens.subtitle_preempt` owns reading speed, and a `rhythm.` card that points at either is naming an owner, not offering you a choice. And **distrust axis one whenever your honest answer is its first value** — nearly three-quarters of the shelf lives on the page, so on a print-first piece this map has two questions left and is doing two-thirds of the work it does on a script.
**Prompt:** `[Selector — produces no prompt. It returns card ids. The chosen card carries the prompt.]`

---

**The axes**

**Axis 1 — Who sets the pace: the reader, a voice, or a clock nobody in the room controls?**
Asked first, because it is the condition the shelf repeats most and the only one that can disqualify a card outright. At least eighteen `Yields to:` lines turn on the channel, and eleven of them name **a different card on this shelf** as the replacement: *"where they have to hear it"* (`rhythm.periodic_sentence`), *"for the ear, for translation, or for anyone reading at speed"* (`rhythm.embedding_load`), *"Spoken piece; the listener cannot see quote marks"* (`rhythm.quotation_weight`), *"wherever the piece is spoken"* (`rhythm.parenthesis_aside`), *"Narration for the ear; repeated openings read as error"* (`rhythm.anaphora`), *"in voice-over it does not exist at all"* (`rhythm.semicolon_balance`), *"where the piece is read aloud"* (`rhythm.subordination_delay`), *"where the book is a read-aloud rather than a read-alone"* (`rhythm.decodable_text`), *"where the piece will be subtitled rather than dubbed"* (`rhythm.lip_sync_adaptation`), *"where the script drives the shoot"* (`rhythm.locked_picture_narration`), and the reverse of all of them in `rhythm.narrator_paragraph`: *"where the print edition is the primary object and the audio is a by-product"*.

**Axis 2 — What is the unit you are actually shaping: the sentence, the block, or the whole of it?**
This is the axis that never fails, because every card on the shelf is about exactly one size of thing and the shelf argues about size constantly: *"The discontinuity is larger than a paragraph"* (`rhythm.paragraph_break_cut`), *"The shift is too small for white space"* (`rhythm.section_break_scale`), *"A shift that does not earn a chapter"* (`rhythm.chapter_as_unit`), *"The line cannot survive isolation; land it in-paragraph"* (`rhythm.one_line_paragraph`), *"Diagnosing block rhythm by eye rather than numbers"* (`rhythm.paragraph_breath`), *"where the subject genuinely requires sustained argument"* (`rhythm.white_space`). Three of those form a closed loop between neighbouring sizes, which is the shape of an axis rather than a leaf: the cards are not disagreeing about the device, they are disagreeing about the unit.

**Axis 3 — Does the sentence answer to anything outside its own effect?**
Asked last and asked as a gate. Nine conditions turn on an obligation the prose did not choose: *"where the reader has to act on the sentence"* (`rhythm.periodic_sentence`), *"wherever the connective carries legal or logical force"* (`rhythm.conjunction_control`), *"where the material is legal, contested, or about the speaker's own reliability"* (`rhythm.translated_rhythm`), *"where the disclosure is legally prescribed verbatim and you have no authority over the wording"* (`rhythm.disclosure_as_content`), *"where the list is information the reader must retain or act on"* (`rhythm.list_accumulation`), *"the piece is edited to a house style … a splice is read as a typo rather than a choice"* (`rhythm.comma_splice_tool`), *"where there is genuinely one duration and one placement"* (`rhythm.cutdown_ladder`). It is asked last because a *yes* does not pick a card — it removes most of them, and what is left is the block that was written for somebody else's constraint.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `rhythm.length_as_tempo` governing the passage, with `rhythm.short_after_long` on the turn — and it is argued from the shelf, not asserted.** `rhythm.length_as_tempo` is the only technique card here whose absence has a named failure of its own: `rhythm.monotone_length` exists solely to describe prose written without it, and its `Yields to:` names `rhythm.length_as_tempo` with the word *always*, which nothing else on this shelf says about any live card. `rhythm.short_after_long` is where the shelf sends the biggest gesture on the page when that gesture will not carry — *"The line cannot survive isolation; land it in-paragraph"* (`rhythm.one_line_paragraph`) — which makes it the shelf's own fallback for a beat that needs landing. Together they are also the most worn pair in English prose instruction, and that is exactly why they are named as the default rather than as the answer.

**The one against it is `rhythm.entryless_loop`.** Nothing routes to it; it is named by no `Yields to:` on this shelf; and it is the only card here that removes the assumption every other card is built on — that the audience is present for the first sentence. Every other withholding or delaying device (`rhythm.periodic_sentence`, `rhythm.withheld_subject`, `rhythm.subordination_delay`, `rhythm.last_word_turn`) spends an opening in order to buy an ending, which is a debt the shelf assumes the audience will stay to collect. `rhythm.entryless_loop` never takes the loan. Its stated cost is precise and bounded — it *"costs you every tool that depends on setup"* — and on a screen nobody chose to start, that setup was never going to be watched. Its near cousin against the grain is `rhythm.found_document_rhythm`, where the rhythm is deliberately somebody else's and deliberately worse than yours, and which likewise nothing on this shelf yields to.

**The unasked**

**Thirty of the seventy-one reachable cards are the target of no `Yields to:` field anywhere on this shelf.** They can be chosen but nothing ever sends you to them. By id:

`rhythm.short_short_long` · `rhythm.last_word_turn` · `rhythm.end_weight` · `rhythm.one_line_paragraph` · `rhythm.triad` · `rhythm.list_accumulation` · `rhythm.consonant_texture` · `rhythm.saxon_vs_latinate` · `rhythm.verb_load` · `rhythm.adverb_discipline` · `rhythm.colon_drop` · `rhythm.read_aloud_test` · `rhythm.loose_sentence` · `rhythm.ellipsis_trail` · `rhythm.question_rhythm` · `rhythm.quotation_weight` · `rhythm.chiasmus` · `rhythm.conjunction_control` · `rhythm.epistrophe` · `rhythm.tricolon_crescens` · `rhythm.chapter_as_unit` · `rhythm.book_level_pace` · `rhythm.found_document_rhythm` · `rhythm.arabic_rtl_rhythm` · `rhythm.tic_audit` · `rhythm.locked_picture_narration` · `rhythm.cutdown_ladder` · `rhythm.decodable_text` · `rhythm.entryless_loop` · `rhythm.disclosure_as_content`

**And the shape of that list is the finding, not its length.** There are two shapes in it, and each names a card the shelf is missing.

**First: the whole commercial-constraint region is unasked, and the reason is dated.** The shelf's third file holds writing to a fixed duration, the levelled text, and rhythm under commercial constraint — and five of its nine reachable cards are on the list above, with the rest reached almost entirely by each other. **Exactly one arrow crosses into that file from the other two**, `rhythm.instruction_step` to `rhythm.call_to_action_line`. The file's own coverage note records why without drawing the conclusion: the category was written to a stated target of seventy-five, the pair fields were written against the shelf as it then stood, and the target later moved to eighty-two. **The pair graph is a map of a smaller shelf.** So a writer holding a sixty-second slot, a locked picture or a public screen is never sent to the card written for them — they have to already know it exists, which is the one thing a writer under a commercial constraint does not.

**Second: the figure ladder only runs downward.** Every arrow among the rhetorical figures points from the more elaborate device to the plainer one — `rhythm.chiasmus` down to `rhythm.antithesis_balance`, `rhythm.antithesis_balance` down to `rhythm.parallel_construction`, `rhythm.triad` down to `rhythm.parallel_construction`, `rhythm.epistrophe` across to `rhythm.anaphora`, `rhythm.tricolon_crescens` out of the shelf entirely to `comedy.rule_of_three`. **Nothing on this shelf ever tells a writer to raise a sentence.** The pair field can only express *this is too much for here*; it has no form for *this is not enough for here*, because the readers who wrote these fields were each holding one card and asking where it stops — and a card does not stop by being too plain. That is why `rhythm.empty_music`, a sentence with perfect rhythm and no content, is a failure the shelf catches by name, while the flat sentence that should have been a figure has no name here at all. **The card this shelf wants is the up-rung: the one that says a plain sentence is under-built for the weight it is carrying, and names the figure to raise it to.** The nearest thing that exists is `rhythm.last_word_turn`, which describes the raised version — and it is itself unasked.

`rhythm.who_sets_the_pace`

### The Periodic Sentence

**Also called:** the suspended sentence, the grand-style period, the delayed main clause
**What it is:** A sentence that holds its main clause until the end, so the reader carries the subordinate material without knowing yet what it is for. The meaning closes on the last few words.
**Effect on the audience:** Suspense inside a single sentence. The reader is held under load, then released, and the release feels like a verdict rather than a statement.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it once in a section, on the sentence that passes judgement — the cause of a collapse, the reason a family left, the thing that was decided. The craft rule is that the front load must be parallel and the main clause must be short: two or three matched subordinate units, then five or six words that close. If the front load is a jumble of unlike clauses, the reader is holding luggage, not tension. It is the formal opposite of `rhythm.loose_sentence` and the long-form cousin of `rhythm.last_word_turn`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Novel, Voiceover Script, Documentary, Memoir | genres: Literary, Historical, Heritage, Journalism
**Avoid when:** The reader has to act on the sentence, or hear it. In instructions, safety copy and legal drafting the delayed main clause is the single worst structure available, and in audio the listener has nothing to hold the suspended material in — see `rhythm.listener_no_rewind`.
**Example:**
> Because the river moved, because the canal silted a metre every decade, because the grain that fed thirty thousand people had to come further every year and finally further than anyone could carry it, the city was abandoned.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.instruction_step` where the reader has to act on the sentence, and `rhythm.listener_no_rewind` where they have to hear it. In instructions, safety copy and legal drafting the delayed main clause is the worst structure available, and in audio the listener has nothing to hold the suspended material in.  
`rhythm.periodic_sentence`

---

### The Loose Sentence

**Also called:** the right-branching sentence, the trailing sentence, the additive sentence
**What it is:** The main clause comes first and everything after it is addition. The sentence is grammatically complete early, and could be stopped at several points without breaking.
**Effect on the audience:** Ease. It reads like speech, because speech is built this way, and the reader is never holding anything unresolved.
**Used for and where it works best:** This is your default gear and should be most of your prose. Use it for narration, for reportage, for anything conversational. The craft rule is that because the sentence completes early, every trailing element has to add a new fact — a loose sentence that trails into restatement is where slack prose comes from. And the reader still hears the last phrase as the point, so put the thing that matters last even though the grammar stopped needing it: `rhythm.end_weight`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Essay, Podcast, Voiceover Script | genres: all
**Avoid when:** You need the reader held. A page of loose sentences reads relaxed to the point of slack, and nothing in it can land — which is why one periodic sentence in a loose passage hits so hard.
**Example:**
> She kept the shop open through the whole of that winter, on half stock, with the shutters down by four, serving the same eleven customers who had come since her father's time and who all now bought less than they used to.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.periodic_sentence` — where you need the reader held. A page of loose sentences reads relaxed to the point of slack and nothing in it can land, which is exactly why one periodic sentence in a loose passage hits so hard.  
`rhythm.loose_sentence`

### Building a Cumulative Sentence

**Also called:** the Christensen sentence, base clause plus free modifiers, levels of generality
**What it is:** A construction method, not an effect: write a plain base clause that could stand alone, then hang free modifiers off it, each one attaching to what came before and moving one step down in generality — whole, then part, then detail.
**Effect on the audience:** The reader watches something come into focus. Each modifier narrows, so attention tightens rather than wandering, which is why a long cumulative sentence does not feel long.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it to describe anything the reader must see clearly — a face, a room, a landscape, a body doing work. The craft rule is the ladder: never let two consecutive modifiers sit at the same level of generality, because two equal modifiers read as a list and the sentence stops descending. Cover the base clause with your thumb; if what remains is a pile of adjectives, you have written decoration. `rhythm.long_breath` is what this sentence feels like; this card is how it is built.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Essay, Documentary | genres: Literary, Historical, Heritage, Drama
**Avoid when:** The detail does not reward the descent. A cumulative sentence promises that the closer you look the more there is, so it is a lie when the last modifier is the least interesting thing in it.
**Example:**
> He was working the lathe, both hands on the rest, shoulders squared against the vibration, one thumbnail black from a job he had never explained.

`rhythm.cumulative_build`

---

### Subordination as Delay

**Also called:** hypotaxis against parataxis, clause stacking, the held clause
**What it is:** Choosing whether to rank your clauses (subordination — "although", "because", "which") or to lay them side by side (coordination and full stops). Subordination postpones the sentence's resolution; coordination does not.
**Effect on the audience:** Hypotactic prose reads as a mind analysing, qualifying, arguing with itself. Paratactic prose reads as events happening. The same content, reordered, changes what kind of person seems to be speaking.
**Used for and where it works best:** Match the syntax to the mental state. A character reasoning gets subordination; a character acting gets parataxis. The craft rule is a ceiling: one level of subordination is invisible, two is felt, three is work — and at three, one of those clauses wants to be its own sentence. In non-fiction, subordination is where you hide your weakest claim, so audit your "although" clauses for things you would not say in a main clause.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Novel, Memoir, Documentary, One-Hour Drama | genres: Literary, Journalism, Social Drama, Historical
**Avoid when:** The piece is being read aloud or translated. Subordinate chains are the first thing that breaks in the ear (`rhythm.performed_breath`) and the first thing a translator has to rebuild (`rhythm.write_for_translator`).
**Example:**
> Paratactic: "The loan was refused. He sold the van. The work went to a firm in Mosul."
>
> Hypotactic: "Because the loan was refused, he sold the van, which meant the work went, as everyone had said it would, to a firm in Mosul."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.performed_breath` where the piece is read aloud, and `rhythm.write_for_translator` where it will be translated. Subordinate chains are the first thing that breaks in the ear and the first thing a translator has to rebuild.  
`rhythm.subordination_delay`

---

### The Sentence That Withholds Its Subject

**Also called:** the left-branching sentence, the fronted adverbial, front-loading
**What it is:** Putting the time, the place or the condition before the subject, so the reader has the frame before they have the actor.
**Effect on the audience:** The subject lands as an arrival. The reader has already built the room, and then someone walks into it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it to set a scene in one sentence, to mark a time jump without a section break, or to make an ordinary subject significant by making the reader wait two beats for it. The craft rule is a weight limit: keep the front load under about a dozen words and make sure it contains no noun that could be mistaken for the real subject, or the reader parses it wrongly and has to start again. Fronting and end-weight are the same instrument from opposite ends — see `rhythm.end_weight` and, for the deliberate version stretched across a paragraph, `info.delayed_decoding`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Essay, Documentary, Voiceover Script | genres: Literary, Thriller, Heritage, Historical, Crime
**Avoid when:** Every paragraph opens this way. Three fronted adverbials in a row is a tic with a formal name, and it makes prose sound like a minutes book: "On Tuesday... At the meeting... Following the vote..."
**Example:**
> Before: "The site foreman was standing at the fence when they arrived at six, in the rain, after the gate had been cut."
>
> After: "At six, in the rain, with the gate already cut, the site foreman was standing at the fence."

`rhythm.withheld_subject`

---

### Embedding and What a Reader Can Hold

**Also called:** centre-embedding, the interrupted spine, nested clauses
**What it is:** Putting material between a subject and its verb, so the reader must hold the subject in working memory until the verb arrives and completes it.
**Effect on the audience:** Cost, paid silently. One embedding is free. Two is a reread. Three is a sentence nobody finishes, however grammatical it is.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use a single short embedding to add a necessary qualification without starting a new sentence — and that is the whole legitimate use. The craft rule is measurable: count the words between the subject and its verb, and treat anything over about eight as a leak. The fix is almost always to move the embedded material to the front (`rhythm.withheld_subject`) or the end (`rhythm.loose_sentence`), where it costs nothing. `rhythm.read_aloud_test` finds these faster than any other method, because your lungs find the gap before your eye does.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Novel, Documentary, Explainer | genres: Literary, Journalism, Educational
**Avoid when:** You are writing for the ear, for translation, or for anyone reading at speed. Embedding is the main reason competent official prose is unreadable, and it is the fault that survives every other kind of editing because each individual word is correct.
**Example:**
> Before: "The report the committee the minister appointed produced was ignored."
>
> After: "The minister appointed a committee. The committee produced a report. Nobody read it."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.listener_no_rewind` — for the ear, for translation, or for anyone reading at speed. Embedding is the main reason competent official prose is unreadable, and it survives every other kind of editing because each individual word is correct.  
`rhythm.embedding_load`

## More Punctuation

### The Semicolon and What It Actually Does

**Also called:** the half-stop, the balance mark, the fulcrum
**What it is:** A mark that joins two independent clauses into one sentence with two halves. It pauses harder than a comma and softer than a full stop, and unlike either it asserts that the two halves belong together.
**Effect on the audience:** Poise. A full stop divides two statements; a semicolon makes the reader weigh them against each other, so the second half is heard as consequence, mirror or contradiction of the first.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when the second clause is the other side of the first and you want them read in one movement. The craft rule is balance: the two halves should be close to the same length, because the semicolon is a fulcrum and a short clause propped against a long one wobbles. Budget two per essay and none in a chase. The semicolon separating items in a complicated list is administration, not rhythm, and does not count against the budget. It is the natural mark for `rhythm.antithesis_balance`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Novel, Memoir, Documentary | genres: Literary, Journalism, Historical, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The register is fast, commercial or hard-boiled, or the copy will be spoken. In a thriller a semicolon reads as the author clearing his throat, and in voice-over it does not exist at all — the narrator will give you a comma or a full stop and nothing in between.
**Example:**
> Before: "The excavation was funded for three seasons. Only one season was completed, and that was because of the war."
>
> After: "The excavation was funded for three seasons; the war allowed it one."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.full_stop_tempo` — in a fast, commercial or hard-boiled register, and in anything spoken. A semicolon reads as the author clearing his throat there, and in voice-over it does not exist at all: the narrator will give you a comma or a full stop and nothing in between.  
`rhythm.semicolon_balance`

---

### The Ellipsis

**Also called:** suspension points, the trail-off, the fade
**What it is:** Three dots marking a line that fades rather than stops. In dialogue it is the standard mark for trailing away, against the dash for being cut off.
**Effect on the audience:** Hesitation. The reader slows at the dots and finishes the sentence themselves, which is either intimacy or irritation depending on whether they can.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it where a speaker runs out — of nerve, of information, of the will to say the rest — and where the reader can supply what is missing. The craft rule is that an ellipsis must have something to trail into: if the reader cannot complete the line, the dots are atmosphere with no content. One per scene. Never combine it with a dash, and never use it inside narration as a general-purpose pause; that is what `rhythm.full_stop_tempo` and a paragraph break are for. Against interruption, see `rhythm.dash_interrupt` and `dial.interruption`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Stage Play, Audio Drama, Comics | genres: Drama, Romance, Literary, Horror
**Avoid when:** You are using it to make a flat line sound significant. Dots do not add mystery to a sentence that has none; they only tell the reader that you wanted the sentence to be mysterious.
**Example:**
> "I told them I'd been there since the Tuesday." She looked at the tablecloth. "Which was true, in a way, because the Monday I was..."
>
> Nobody asked her to finish it.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.dash_interrupt` — The speaker is cut off, not trailing away.  
`rhythm.ellipsis_trail`

---

### Parentheses as an Aside Voice

**Also called:** the bracketed aside, the whisper, the quiet parenthesis
**What it is:** Material set inside round brackets, which the reader hears in a lower, faster, private voice — as against a pair of dashes, which makes the same aside loud.
**Effect on the audience:** A second speaker appears inside the sentence. Brackets read as confiding, sometimes as comic, always as lower status than the main clause.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use them when the narrator wants to say something to the reader that the sentence itself would not say — a correction, an admission, a joke at the narrator's expense. The craft rule is droppability: cut the bracket and the sentence must still stand, or the brackets are hiding a structural fault. The second rule is register: the aside must sound different from the prose around it, or it is only a comma with ambition. Compare `rhythm.dash_interrupt` for the loud version and `voice.confiding_voice` for the persona this builds.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Memoir, Novel, Comics | genres: Comedy, Literary, Journalism, Drama
**Avoid when:** The piece is spoken. Brackets have no audible form, so an audiobook or voice-over narrator must either flatten them (losing the joke) or perform them (over-signalling it). Rewrite the aside as its own short sentence — see `rhythm.narrator_paragraph`.
**Example:**
> He had been on the committee for nineteen years (twenty, if you count the year he was suspended, and he did count it) and had never once voted against a proposal from the chair.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.narrator_paragraph` — wherever the piece is spoken. Brackets have no audible form, so a narrator must either flatten them and lose the joke or perform them and over-signal it; rewrite the aside as its own short sentence.  
`rhythm.parenthesis_aside`

---

### The Question Mark's Rhythm

**Also called:** the interrogative beat, the rhetorical question, the turned-up line
**What it is:** A question inside prose changes the contour of the line — the pitch rises, the sentence opens instead of closing, and the reader is handed a job.
**Effect on the audience:** Attention spikes, because a question is the one punctuation the reader has to answer. It also breaks the declarative beat of a paragraph more completely than any length change can.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use one question to turn a paragraph, and put it where you want the reader to stop agreeing and start thinking. The craft rule is that a question is a debt: answer it within the same section or make it plain you never will — an unanswered question the reader believes was accidental reads as sloppiness, and an unanswered question the reader believes was deliberate reads as depth. See `scene.close_on_question` and `open.question_planted_first` for the structural versions.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Documentary, Podcast, Explainer, Voiceover Script | genres: Journalism, Documentary, Educational, Literary
**Avoid when:** The questions are doing the work of transitions. "So what does this mean?" and "But is that the whole story?" are throat-clearing with a hook on the end, and three of them in a piece makes an essay sound like it is interviewing itself.
**Example:**
> Before: "It is important to consider who benefited from the sale of the site."
>
> After: "The site sold for a tenth of its assessed value. Who bought it? A company registered eleven days earlier, at an address that turned out to be a barber's shop."

`rhythm.question_rhythm`

---

### Quotation and Its Weight

**Also called:** the quoted sentence, quoting inside your prose, the block quote
**What it is:** A quotation arrives inside your prose in a different voice, and the reader's pace changes for the length of it. Quotation marks are a rhythm instruction as much as an attribution.
**Effect on the audience:** Slowing and heightened credence. The reader treats quoted words as evidence and reads them more carefully than your own, which is a gift when the quote is good and a hole in the page when it is not.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use a short quotation where the exact words matter and paraphrase everywhere else. The craft rule is about placement: attribute first when the speaker is the point, attribute after when the words are the point, and never let a quotation run longer than the sentence that introduced it unless the quotation is the payoff. Ending a paragraph on a quote is the strongest position you have, so spend it only on a line better than anything you would write. See `info.the_document` and `voice.found_document`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Documentary, Podcast, Memoir | genres: Journalism, Documentary, Heritage, Historical
**Avoid when:** You are quoting to fill. A long block quote in a rhythm-driven piece hands your pacing to someone who was not trying to write — and in a spoken piece, an unmarked quotation is simply confusing, because the listener cannot see the marks.
**Example:**
> Before: "The curator explained that in her view the objects had been removed without any legal authority whatsoever and that this had been known for decades."
>
> After: "The curator had one sentence for it. 'They were taken, and everyone knew.'"

**Yields to:** `rhythm.listener_no_rewind` — Spoken piece; the listener cannot see quote marks.  
`rhythm.quotation_weight`

---

## Classical Figures That Still Work

### Chiasmus

**Also called:** antimetabole, the ABBA reversal, the crossed sentence
**What it is:** Repeating a pair of terms in reverse order across the two halves of a sentence, so the second half mirrors the first.
**Effect on the audience:** Closure that feels like proof. The shape is so finished that readers accept the claim as demonstrated when nothing has been demonstrated at all — which is why it is the default shape of aphorisms and of political slogans.
**Used for and where it works best:** Spend it once, in a last paragraph, on a claim you can defend. The craft rule is that the reversal must reverse the meaning as well as the words: if the second half says nothing the first half did not, you have written decoration in a clever shape. Short terms only — a chiasmus with a four-word limb collapses. See `end.last_line`, and `rhythm.antithesis_balance` for the version that does not cross.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Voiceover Script, Song Lyric, Memoir | genres: Literary, Heritage, Historical, Comedy
**Avoid when:** The piece is reported, technical or contemporary-realist. Chiasmus is rare in modern speech, so it always announces itself, and in journalism readers hear it as the writer reaching for applause in the middle of a fact.
**Example:**
> He worked to live at twenty and lived to work at fifty, and could not say which year the swap had happened in.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.antithesis_balance` — Reported or technical register; use the uncrossed version.  
`rhythm.chiasmus`

---

### Conjunction Control Beyond the List

**Also called:** clause-level asyndeton and polysyndeton, dropping the "and", the doubled connective
**What it is:** Controlling conjunctions between whole clauses and sentences rather than between list items: stripping them out so statements butt against each other, or putting "and" at the head of sentence after sentence.
**Effect on the audience:** Stripped conjunctions read as compression and verdict — the reader supplies the logic and therefore believes it. Doubled conjunctions read as endurance, scripture or a child telling you what happened, because every clause is granted equal weight.
**Used for and where it works best:** Decide at paragraph scale and hold it for the whole paragraph; switching halfway reads as an error, not a modulation. Stripped conjunctions suit aftermath, testimony and anything you want heard as a finding. Doubled conjunctions need a subject that earns the register — ritual, childhood, exhaustion, a journey that would not end. See `voice.incantatory_register`, and `rhythm.list_accumulation` for the same instrument applied inside a single list.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Memoir, Essay, Voiceover Script, Documentary | genres: Literary, Heritage, Historical, Horror, Drama
**Avoid when:** The connective carries legal or logical force. In `rhythm.legal_sentence` and in instructions, "and" versus "or" versus nothing at all changes what the sentence permits, and a dropped conjunction there is not a rhythm choice, it is an ambiguity.
**Example:**
> Stripped: "The pump failed in June. The council was told in July. The wells went dry in August. Nobody was dismissed."
>
> Doubled: "And they walked out past the checkpoint and nobody stopped them and nobody spoke and the road went on being the road for another eleven hours."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.legal_sentence` and `rhythm.instruction_step` — wherever the connective carries legal or logical force. There "and" against "or" against nothing at all changes what the sentence permits, and a dropped conjunction is an ambiguity rather than a rhythm choice.  
`rhythm.conjunction_control`

---

### Epistrophe

**Also called:** terminal repetition, the repeated tail, epiphora
**What it is:** Repeating the same word or short phrase at the end of successive clauses or sentences — the mirror image of anaphora.
**Effect on the audience:** Heavier than anaphora and more final. The ear remembers ends, so a repeated tail accumulates like a refrain and the last instance arrives as a verdict rather than a beat.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it to close an argument, not to open one. The craft rule is that the repeated phrase must be short and land on a stress — one or two words, ideally a concrete noun or a Saxon verb, because a repeated abstraction ("...for the community. ...for the community.") goes soft on the second pass. Three limbs. If you use both figures, run `rhythm.anaphora` first to build and epistrophe second to close; the machinery is `rhythm.end_weight`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Voiceover Script, Stage Play, Song Lyric, Documentary | genres: Literary, Social Drama, Heritage, Journalism
**Avoid when:** The tail phrase is not the point of every limb. Forcing three unlike clauses to end on the same words makes the figure argue for you, and a reader who notices that has stopped listening to the content — `rhythm.audible_technique`.
**Example:**
> The paperwork was in order. The permits were in order. The trucks came at two in the morning and the site was levelled by six, and all of it, every signature and every load, was in order.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.anaphora` — Opening an argument rather than closing one.  
`rhythm.epistrophe`

---

### Antithesis and the Balanced Sentence

**Also called:** the balanced sentence, isocolon with contrast, the scales
**What it is:** Two limbs of similar shape and similar length holding opposed content, so the grammar itself performs the opposition.
**Effect on the audience:** The contrast feels proven. Matched structure makes the reader accept the two halves as commensurable, which is exactly what a symmetrical sentence is asserting.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it on a genuine opposition you want remembered: cost against benefit, then against now, what was promised against what arrived. The craft rule is to balance by syllable count as well as by grammar — count them, and if one limb runs four syllables longer, cut it, because the ear hears the imbalance as a weaker claim. A balanced sentence is where `rhythm.semicolon_balance` earns its keep, and it is the un-crossed relative of `rhythm.chiasmus`. Related: `rhythm.parallel_construction`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Voiceover Script, Documentary, Novel | genres: Literary, Journalism, Historical, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The two halves are not actually opposed, or not actually equal. False balance is the professional hazard here: a beautifully weighted sentence that gives a documented fact and an unevidenced denial the same syllable count has told the reader they are the same size, and in journalism that is a lie the rhythm told.
**Example:**
> Before: "The first restoration was done properly, whereas the second one was mostly about the money and it also caused a lot of damage."
>
> After: "The first restoration saved the wall; the second one sold it."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.parallel_construction` — The limbs are matched but not opposed.  
`rhythm.antithesis_balance`

---

### Tricolon Crescens and Its Opposite

**Also called:** the ascending three, the crescendo triple, tricolon diminuens
**What it is:** A three-part structure measured by syllable weight rather than by item count: short, longer, longest, so the third limb carries a crescendo — or deliberately reversed, longest to shortest, so the sentence deflates.
**Effect on the audience:** Ascending, it lifts and lands, which is why it is the shape of every memorable public sentence. Descending, it drops the floor out, which is why it is the shape of a joke.
**Used for and where it works best:** Count the syllables: something like 2 / 3 / 7 is a crescens and will feel inevitable. Reverse it — 7 / 3 / 2 — and the same content becomes comic or bitter, because the reader was set up for expansion and got a monosyllable. The craft rule is that the direction is a decision, not an accident; if your three items came out 5 / 9 / 4, the sentence is trailing and you have not chosen anything. `rhythm.triad` covers the three-item pattern itself; this card is about which way it leans. For the comic version see `comedy.rule_of_three` and `comedy.funny_word_last`.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Voiceover Script, Song Lyric, Reels/Shorts, Documentary | genres: Comedy, Literary, Journalism, Heritage
**Avoid when:** You are stacking crescens after crescens. Three ascending triples on one page and the reader is riding an escalator; the fourth one gets nothing, and the technique is now audible.
**Example:**
> Crescens: "He lost the job, the flat, and every friend who had ever lent him money."
>
> Diminuens: "He had a plan, a deadline, and nothing."

**Yields to:** `comedy.rule_of_three` — The three-parter is a joke; comic timing owns it.  
`rhythm.tricolon_crescens`

---

## Paragraph and Chapter Pace

### The Paragraph as a Unit of Breath

**Also called:** paragraph length as pacing, one move per paragraph, the breath block
**What it is:** Treating each paragraph as a single breath of argument or action — one move, taken at one pace — and treating the sequence of paragraph lengths as a rhythm in its own right.
**Effect on the audience:** Readers do not consciously register paragraph length, but they pace themselves by it, and they use the break as permission to look up. A run of same-sized paragraphs removes that permission and produces the specific fatigue of a page that will not let you go.
**Used for and where it works best:** Write the paragraph to finish its move and stop, then check the run. The craft rule is numerical: write down the sentence count of each paragraph down a chapter — 4, 2, 9, 1, 6, 3 — and look at the series. If there is no 1 and no 9 anywhere in it, the chapter has no dynamics, whatever the content is doing. `rhythm.white_space` is the same diagnostic done by eye; this is the one you can do on a phone.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Essay, Memoir, Short Story, Documentary | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The move genuinely takes nine sentences and you split it for the look of the page. A paragraph broken where the thought does not break makes the reader hunt for a transition that was never there.
**Example:**
> She said no.
>
> He had expected it, had rehearsed the drive home around it, had decided in the car park that the important thing was to hear it without argument, and he did hear it without argument, and then he sat in the corridor for twenty minutes anyway because there was nowhere in the building where a man could stand still without being asked whether he was all right.
>
> Then he went back in and asked again.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.white_space` — Diagnosing block rhythm by eye rather than numbers.  
`rhythm.paragraph_breath`

---

### The Chapter as a Rhythm Unit

**Also called:** chapter length as pace control, the potato-chip chapter, chapter drop
**What it is:** The chapter break is the largest pause you own inside a book, and chapter length is the coarsest pace control. Short chapters accelerate because the reader keeps arriving at a finish line; long chapters slow time and ask for commitment.
**Effect on the audience:** Measurable. Commercial thrillers run three to five pages a chapter precisely because the pages turn faster, and readers consistently read "one more" when one more is two thousand words rather than eight.
**Used for and where it works best:** Set length by the size of what happens — `scene.length_follows_value` — then vary deliberately: a two-page chapter after three long ones reads as an alarm going off. The craft rule is that a chapter must end on a turn and open on movement, because the white space after the last line is the largest emphasis in the book and the first line is competing with the reader's decision to sleep. See `open.chapter_opening`, `seq.chapter_cluster` and `info.cliffhanger_reveal`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Podcast | genres: Thriller, Crime, Literary, Historical, Drama
**Avoid when:** You chop to hit a target. Arbitrary short chapters with no turn in them produce fake pace: the reader notices they are finishing chapters without anything having happened, and the device stops working for the rest of the book.
**Example:**
> Chapter ending, long chapter: "...and by the time the lorries were loaded it was nearly light, and he had still not told her."
>
> Next chapter, opening line: "She found out from the neighbour."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.section_break_scale` — A shift that does not earn a chapter.  
`rhythm.chapter_as_unit`

---

### Section Breaks and White Space at Scale

**Also called:** the space break, the asterisk break, the scene divider
**What it is:** A blank line or a typographic mark inside a chapter, signalling a shift of time, place or viewpoint without the ceremony of a chapter break.
**Effect on the audience:** A held breath and a jump. The reader accepts almost any discontinuity across a section break — hours, years, a change of narrator — because the white space has pre-authorised it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use a break instead of writing a transition; it is the cheapest time jump in prose and always better than "Later that afternoon..." (`time.passage_marker`). The craft rule is that the line before the break and the line after it are the two most-read lines in the chapter — treat them as a chapter ending and a chapter opening in miniature, and leave on the strong one (`scene.early_exit`). Cap it at three or four breaks per chapter; past that the chapter is a list of fragments and the break means nothing. The paragraph-scale version is `rhythm.paragraph_break_cut`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Comics, Essay | genres: Literary, Thriller, Crime, Historical, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The break is doing the work you did not want to do. If you cannot write the connection, a space break hides that from you and not from the reader, who feels the gap as a missing scene rather than as a cut.
**Example:**
> He signed it without reading past the first page.
>
> ⁂
>
> The letter from the ministry took four years to arrive, and by then two of the four signatories were dead.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.paragraph_break_cut` — The shift is too small for white space.  
`rhythm.section_break_scale`

---

### Pace Across a Whole Book

**Also called:** the pace map, macro rhythm, the sagging middle
**What it is:** The rhythm of a long work read at book scale: where you are in scene and where you are in summary, where the chapters get long, where the reader is allowed to rest.
**Effect on the audience:** Readers never describe this accurately. They say "it dragged in the middle" or "the end felt rushed", and what they are describing is a run of same-duration chapters or a compression of the last three turns into one.
**Used for and where it works best:** Build the map in revision, not in drafting: one row per chapter with word count, scene or summary, and what value turned. Three long scene chapters in a row in the middle third is the standard sag, and the cure is a summary chapter, not a shorter one — alternating rendered scene with compressed summary is what makes a book breathe (`time.scene_duration`, `time.summary_duration`). The craft rule is that the last quarter should be your shortest chapters and your fewest summaries. See `seq.act_rhythm`, `seq.length_variation` and `tens.trough_placement`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Memoir, Documentary, One-Hour Drama, Podcast | genres: all
**Avoid when:** You are still drafting. A pace map applied to a first draft makes you fix rhythm in material whose structure has not settled, and you will rewrite it all again — see `rhythm.first_draft_cadence` for the related trap.
**Example:**
> Chapters 11–14 of a draft, mapped: 5,100 words / scene / no turn; 4,800 / scene / no turn; 5,400 / scene / small turn; 4,900 / scene / no turn.
>
> Four chapters, one turn, nineteen thousand words, all at the same duration. Nothing in the prose is wrong. The reader will say the middle dragged, and the reader will be right.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.first_draft_cadence` — Still drafting; set cadence before mapping pace.  
`rhythm.book_level_pace`

---

## Rhythm in Specific Registers

### The Legal or Procedural Sentence

**Also called:** the operative sentence, plain-language drafting, the flat register
**What it is:** A sentence built to be parsed, not heard: one obligation, subject and verb together, conditions moved out into a numbered list instead of embedded in the clause.
**Effect on the audience:** Nothing, deliberately. The reader of a legal or procedural sentence is scanning for who must do what, and any music you add is a signal they have to filter out before they can work.
**Used for and where it works best:** Follow the plain-language benchmarks and stop arguing with them: an average around twenty words, rework anything over about forty-five, one duty per sentence, standard word order, and conditions listed rather than nested (`rhythm.embedding_load` is the fault this register commits most). The craft rule is that variety still matters — an average of twenty means some sentences of eight and some of thirty, not two hundred sentences of twenty, which is `rhythm.monotone_length` in a suit.
**Best in:** formats: Explainer, Documentary, Essay | genres: Educational, Journalism
**Avoid when:** The register leaks into narrative. Institutional syntax in a scene makes everyone sound like a form; when you want that effect, commit to it and name it — see `voice.institutional_voice` and `voice.register_creep`.
**Example:**
> Before: "In the event that the tenant, having been notified in writing by the landlord or the landlord's agent, fails to remedy the breach within the period specified, the landlord may, at the landlord's discretion, terminate."
>
> After: "The landlord must notify the tenant in writing. The notice must give a deadline. If the tenant misses the deadline, the landlord may end the tenancy."

**Yields to:** `voice.institutional_voice` — where the register is leaking into narrative. Institutional syntax in a scene makes everyone sound like a form; when you want that effect, commit to it and name it rather than letting it drift in.  
`rhythm.legal_sentence`

---

### The Instructional Sentence

**Also called:** the step, imperative-first writing, procedure rhythm
**What it is:** A sentence a reader executes while their hands are busy: context first, then one imperative verb, then one action, and nothing else.
**Effect on the audience:** The reader can look away and come back. Instructional rhythm is measured in glances — how much of the sentence survives in memory between the page and the task.
**Used for and where it works best:** Lead with the location and follow with the action ("In the Settings panel, click Save"), keep steps under about fifteen words, and number them so the reader has somewhere to return to. The craft rule is one action per step, always — two actions in one numbered step is the single most common cause of a reader doing the first and forgetting the second. Short simple sentences here are not a style preference; they are error reduction, and they also halve the cost of translating the manual (`rhythm.write_for_translator`). See `expo.procedural_exposition` and `expo.explainer_scaffold`.
**Best in:** formats: Explainer, Documentary, Voiceover Script, Reels/Shorts | genres: Educational
**Avoid when:** The instructions are also selling. Marketing rhythm inside a procedure — the balanced sentence, the triple, the flourish — adds words the reader must discard mid-task, and they will blame the product for it.
**Example:**
> Before: "Once you've made sure the machine is unplugged and cooled down, you can then go ahead and remove the filter housing by turning it anticlockwise, and give it a rinse."
>
> After: "1. Unplug the machine. 2. Wait ten minutes. 3. Turn the filter housing anticlockwise and lift it out. 4. Rinse it under cold water."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.call_to_action_line` — where the instructions are also selling. Marketing rhythm inside a procedure adds words the reader must discard mid-task, and they will blame the product for it; keep the ask as its own line.  
`rhythm.instruction_step`

---

### The Interview Transcript, Cleaned or Not

**Also called:** clean verbatim, tidying quotes, the transcript pass
**What it is:** Deciding how much of a real person's speech rhythm you keep. True verbatim keeps every "um" and false start; clean verbatim removes fillers and stutters; an edited transcript rewrites for readability and discards the speaker's rhythm entirely.
**Effect on the audience:** Fillers removed, a speaker sounds more competent and more like the writer. Fillers kept, they sound more real and, unfairly, less credible. Neither version is neutral, so the choice is editorial and should be made once, on purpose.
**Used for and where it works best:** Clean verbatim is the working default for features, documentary and podcast: strip "um", "you know", repeated false starts, and keep everything else. The craft rule is the line nobody should cross — you may remove, you may not reorder. Moving a clause inside a quotation changes what the speaker emphasised, and emphasis is the only rhythm a quotation carries. Keep one hesitation exactly where the hesitation is the information. See `info.interview_admission` and `rhythm.quotation_weight`.
**Best in:** formats: Documentary, Podcast, Essay, Memoir | genres: Journalism, Documentary, Heritage, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The material is legal, contested, or about the speaker's own reliability. There you publish verbatim and let the reader hear the mess, because the tidying is itself a claim about the person.
**Example:**
> Verbatim: "We — I mean, the thing is, we, we didn't, um, nobody actually told us. Nobody. So."
>
> Clean verbatim: "We didn't — nobody actually told us. Nobody. So."
>
> Edited (and now a different man): "We were never informed."

`rhythm.transcript_clean`

---

### The Found Document

**Also called:** the inserted document, the diegetic text block, the letter on the page
**What it is:** A letter, ledger, sign, report or message reproduced inside the narration, carrying its own register and therefore its own rhythm.
**Effect on the audience:** The reader slows and believes. A document reads as evidence, and its different pace acts on the page the way a cutaway acts in film.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it where you want the reader to do the interpreting — a document states and the reader concludes, which is faster and more convincing than narration explaining. The craft rule is that the document must not sound like you: flatter, more clipped, with the conventions and small errors of its real register left in place. Keep it short — two hundred words is a long document on a page — and never explain it in the paragraph after; the gap between the document's rhythm and yours is the effect. See `pov.found_document`, `voice.found_document` and `expo.diegetic_text`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Documentary, Comics, Memoir | genres: Crime, Historical, Heritage, Thriller, Horror
**Avoid when:** The document is a lore dump in costume. If it exists only to deliver information the scene could not, the register is fake and readers hear it immediately — `expo.lore_dump`.
**Example:**
> He found the inventory in the back of the file, typed, with a carbon smudge across the date.
>
> *Item 14. Limestone relief, fragmentary, approx. 40 x 60 cm. Condition: chipped lower left. Provenance: local purchase. Value: nominal.*
>
> The relief was in a museum in Frankfurt by the following spring.

`rhythm.found_document_rhythm`

---

## Rhythm Across Languages

### What Actually Survives Translation

**Also called:** the translatable inventory, portable rhythm, effect triage
**What it is:** Sorting your rhythmic effects into those that cross a language boundary and those that do not, before you decide which ones to rely on.
**Effect on the audience:** In the source language, none — this is a planning instrument. In the target language it is the difference between a translation that reads as writing and one that reads as a conversion.
**Used for and where it works best:** The list is short and worth memorising. What crosses: sentence-length variation, paragraph shape, the order of information, the position of the sting, repetition and anaphora, concreteness, the short sentence after the long one. What does not: stress pattern, consonant texture, syllable count, the monosyllabic close, rhyme, alliteration, idiom, and any joke that depends on a word's length. The craft rule is to put the effects that cross into the structure and the effects that do not into individual sentences you can afford to lose. If your paragraph only works because the last word is one syllable, it is untranslatable — which is fine for an English-only essay and wrong for a heritage film that will be subtitled into Arabic. See `rhythm.translated_rhythm`, `lyric.singable_translation`, `dial.subtitle_constraint`.
**Best in:** formats: Documentary, Voiceover Script, Essay, Song Lyric, Explainer | genres: Heritage, Documentary, Journalism, Educational
**Avoid when:** The work is monolingual by design and always will be. Writing defensively for a translation that will never happen costs you the sound-level effects that are half of English prose.
**Example:**
> Survives: "They came for the archive first. Then the school. Then the name of the street."
>
> Does not survive: "The last of the kilns went cold, and the town with it." (The effect is the stressed monosyllable "cold" against the trailing "with it" — in most target languages that stress pattern is gone and only the statement remains.)

**Yields to:** `rhythm.stress_pattern` — Monolingual by design; spend the sound-level effects.  
`rhythm.translation_survivors`

---

### Arabic and Other Right-to-Left Rhythm

**Also called:** RTL prose rhythm, saj' and parallelism, the coordinated sentence
**What it is:** Arabic literary prose builds rhythm from coordination, parallelism and balanced word-counts rather than from the short-sentence contrast that carries English. Classical saj' measures its units in words, not syllables, and pairs them by balance and by end-rhyme.
**Effect on the audience:** An Arabic reader hears authority in coordination and in matched limbs, and hears a chain of clipped five-word sentences as a translated press release, not as urgency.
**Used for and where it works best:** When writing or scripting in Arabic, build the paragraph out of paired, weight-matched clauses joined with the connective, and save the short sentence for the turn — it is your rarest effect there, not your default one. The craft rule for bilingual work: never port the English pacing scheme across, re-score the paragraph (`rhythm.translated_rhythm`), and when you burn subtitles, break the RTL lines at the same syntactic joints you would respect in English — article with noun, preposition with phrase (`rhythm.subtitle_beat`, `dial.subtitle_constraint`). See also `voice.second_language_voice` and `sub.across_languages`.
**Best in:** formats: Voiceover Script, Documentary, Essay, Song Lyric, Explainer | genres: Heritage, Historical, Documentary, Literary
**Avoid when:** You reach for full saj' in modern material. Sustained rhymed prose in a contemporary documentary voice-over sounds like a sermon, and unless that is exactly the register you want, the audience will hear the form and not the content.
**Example:**
> English pacing forced into Arabic, then read back literally: "The city fell. The walls broke. Nobody came." — three flat statements, no balance, no connective; in Arabic it scans as a bulletin.
>
> Re-scored on Arabic terms, read back: "The walls were breached and the gates were opened, and of all the cities that had sworn to send men, not one sent a man." — paired limbs, coordination carrying the sentence, the turn held to the end.

**Yields to:** `voice.incantatory_register` — Sustained rhymed prose; the sermon register is wanted.  
`rhythm.arabic_rtl_rhythm`

---

### The Translated Sentence That Scans Wrong

**Also called:** translationese, source-syntax shadow, the accurate sentence nobody would write
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A translation in which every word is right and the rhythm belongs to the other language: long noun phrases where the target would use a verb, connectives chained where the target would stop, and every sentence the same length because each one maps a single source sentence.
**Effect on the audience:** Readers cannot name it and do not try. They say the translation is "stiff", "old-fashioned", or "obviously translated", and they read less of it.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, outside legal and evidentiary translation where the sentence boundary is part of the record. The diagnostic is to read the translation aloud to someone who does not know the source language and mark where they stumble; the stumbles map the places the source syntax is still showing. The fix is the paragraph, not the sentence: preserve the effect across the block and re-split freely inside it, keeping only the position of the sting.
**Example:**
> Translationese: "And it was that after the completion of the construction of the new bridge, the residents of the area, who had been waiting for a long period, expressed their happiness at the matter."
>
> Rebuilt: "The bridge opened in March. People had been waiting eleven years for it. They came out that night and walked across it in both directions, for no reason, until it got cold."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.translated_rhythm` — always, outside legal and evidentiary translation where the sentence boundary is part of the record. The fix is the paragraph, not the sentence: preserve the effect across the block and re-split freely inside it.  
`rhythm.translationese_scan`

---

### Writing for a Translator

**Also called:** translation-ready drafting, source-text discipline, global English
**What it is:** Writing the source text so that its meaning survives a human or machine translation intact, and putting your rhythm only where rhythm can travel.
**Effect on the audience:** In the source, a slightly plainer text. In every target language, a text that reads as written rather than processed — and a translation bill that is smaller, because ambiguity is what costs.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it on anything that will be localised, subtitled, dubbed or read by a non-native audience. The craft rule is a short checklist applied in a dedicated pass: sentences under about twenty-five words, one idea each, subject and verb adjacent, standard word order, no idiom in a load-bearing position, plain verbs instead of phrasal verbs, and no pronoun whose antecedent is more than a sentence away. Then put your rhythm into what crosses — length variation, paragraph shape, the position of the turn (`rhythm.translation_survivors`).
**Best in:** formats: Explainer, Documentary, Voiceover Script, Reels/Shorts, Podcast | genres: Educational, Documentary, Journalism, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The piece is literary and monolingual. Applied to a novel, this checklist produces competent, exportable, characterless prose — the constraint that protects an instruction manual strips a voice.
**Example:**
> Before: "Having rolled out the new onboarding flow, which the team had been sitting on for a while, we're now seeing users get up to speed much faster."
>
> After: "We released the new onboarding flow in May. The team had finished it in February. Since the release, new users reach their first completed task in half the time."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.translation_survivors` — where the piece is literary and monolingual. Applied to a novel the full checklist produces competent, exportable, characterless prose: the constraint that protects an instruction manual strips a voice.  
`rhythm.write_for_translator`

## The Audiobook and the Read-Aloud

### Paragraph Shape for a Narrator

**Also called:** the take, narration blocking, paragraph as performance unit
**What it is:** Shaping paragraphs for someone who will perform them: a clear first sentence that sets pitch and pace, a middle that does not change register, and a last sentence the narrator can land on.
**Effect on the audience:** A listener who never notices the narrator working. Badly shaped paragraphs make a competent professional sound uncertain, and the listener blames the narrator.
**Used for and where it works best:** Give every paragraph one tone. A paragraph that starts ironic and ends grieving forces a mid-block gear change that no read can make sound natural — split it. The craft rule specific to audio: never open two consecutive paragraphs with the same word, because in the ear a repeated opening sounds like an error rather than a figure, which is why `rhythm.anaphora` must be kept tight and deliberate in narration. Put speaker attribution at the start of long speeches, never at the end. See `rhythm.vo_breath_line` and `voice.write_for_the_ear`.
**Best in:** formats: Audiobook, Voiceover Script, Podcast, Audio Drama, Documentary | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The print edition is the primary object and the audio is a by-product. Then you write for the page and let the narrator's director mark the script — do not compromise both.
**Example:**
> Hard to perform: "It was a joke, obviously, and everyone laughed, and then his mother said the thing about the hospital and the table went quiet and nobody looked at anybody for a while."
>
> Performable: "It was a joke, obviously. Everyone laughed.
>
> Then his mother said the thing about the hospital. The table went quiet, and nobody looked at anybody for a while."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.paragraph_breath` — where the print edition is the primary object and the audio is a by-product. Write for the page and let the narrator's director mark the script; do not compromise both.  
`rhythm.narrator_paragraph`

---

### Breath and the Long Sentence in Performance

**Also called:** breath marking, the slash pass, performable length
**What it is:** Testing sentences against a real pair of lungs at performance pace, and rebuilding the ones that cannot be delivered in one or two breaths.
**Effect on the audience:** Audibly calmer narration. A sentence that outruns the narrator's air produces a snatched breath in the middle of a clause, and listeners hear tension that the writing did not intend.
**Used for and where it works best:** Do a dedicated pass with a pencil: put a slash where you would breathe, then read the page aloud at about 150 words a minute. The craft rule is a two-breath ceiling — a sentence needing three breaths needs a full stop, and the usual offender is a trailing "which" clause, which is also the first thing professional narrators mark for splitting in script prep. A long sentence can survive performance if its commas fall at roughly even intervals; an unpunctuated forty-word stretch cannot, whatever its grammar. See `rhythm.read_aloud_test` for the diagnostic and `rhythm.long_breath` for the effect you are protecting.
**Best in:** formats: Audiobook, Voiceover Script, Audio Drama, Stage Play, Podcast | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The breathlessness is the point. A deliberately unbreathable sentence can render panic — once, marked in the script as such, so the narrator plays it rather than fights it.
**Example:**
> Before: "The building, which had been the customs house and then the telephone exchange and which everyone in the town still called the Exchange although it had been neither for forty years, was sold in the autumn."
>
> After: "The building had been the customs house, then the telephone exchange. / Everyone still called it the Exchange. / It had been neither for forty years. / It sold that autumn."

**Source:** reference — ACX (Audible), "Narrate an audiobook", help article, https://help.acx.com/s/article/producing-and-recording-your-audiobook, checked 2026-09-24; states that most performers narrate about 9,300 words per hour (about 155 words a minute), which supports reading the page at about 150 words a minute. The two-breath ceiling is the package's craft rule, not this source's.  
**Yields to:** `rhythm.long_breath` — where the breathlessness is the point. A deliberately unbreathable sentence can render panic once, marked in the script as such so the narrator plays it rather than fights it.  
`rhythm.performed_breath`

---

### What a Listener Cannot Re-Read

**Also called:** the one-pass constraint, comprehension architecture for audio, no going back
**What it is:** Writing under the rule that the audience gets exactly one pass at every sentence, in order, with no ability to glance back at the previous line.
**Effect on the audience:** Comprehension without effort — or, when it is ignored, a listener who quietly stops following and keeps the audio running as noise.
**Used for and where it works best:** Apply it to every spoken format. The craft rule is a set of hard constraints: attribution before the line, never after; no pronoun whose antecedent is more than one sentence back; names repeated more often than a page would tolerate; numbers rounded; lists capped at three items; and the new information at the end of the line where the listener's attention peaks. Anything the listener must hold across two sentences to understand a third has to be restated (`info.recap_without_recap`). Audio also has no margin and no offscreen — see `tens.audio_no_offscreen`.
**Best in:** formats: Audiobook, Podcast, Voiceover Script, Audio Drama, Documentary, Explainer | genres: Documentary, Journalism, Educational, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The text is print-first. These constraints produce prose that looks repetitive and simple on the page, which is why a piece serving both print and audio needs two versions, not one compromise.
**Example:**
> Print version: "Nineteen of the twenty-three sites she had surveyed in 2011 were gone by the time of her second visit; the twentieth was a car park."
>
> Audio version: "She surveyed twenty-three sites in 2011. When she went back, nineteen of them were gone. One of the nineteen was now a car park."

`rhythm.listener_no_rewind`

## Verse and Lyric-Adjacent Prose

### Prose That Borrows Lyric Rhythm

**Also called:** lyric prose, the incantatory passage, verse devices in a prose line
**What it is:** Importing a device from verse or song — a refrain, a fixed line length, a metrical run, a repeated stress pattern — into prose paragraphs.
**Effect on the audience:** Heightening. The reader hears ceremony and slows down, and the passage is remembered out of proportion to its length, which is why it is the standard shape of an opening or a closing in heritage and documentary writing.
**Used for and where it works best:** Borrow one device, not the kit. A refrain works in prose; a rhyme scheme does not. Put the borrowed rhythm where elevation is already expected — the first paragraph of a section, the last paragraph of a chapter, the top and tail of a voice-over — and drop it immediately afterwards, because the effect depends entirely on the plain prose around it. The craft rule is to keep the device countable: if you cannot say in one sentence what you borrowed, you have written mood rather than rhythm. See `lyric.page_lyric`, `lyric.breath_line_length`, `voice.incantatory_register`, `rhythm.anaphora`.
**Best in:** formats: Memoir, Essay, Novel, Voiceover Script, Song Lyric, Poetry | genres: Literary, Heritage, Historical, Drama
**Avoid when:** You are mid-scene, or the rhyme was an accident. Accidental internal rhyme in ordinary narration ("the rain came again on the plain") reads as a mistake, and accidental metre — a run of iambic pentameter in a news feature — reads as parody the moment anyone notices it, and once noticed it cannot be unheard.
**Example:**
> We counted what we could carry, and we carried what we could name.
>
> The lists are in the back of a Bible in a house in Södertälje: twelve families, four villages, one church that is now a shed. My grandmother wrote them in pencil because she expected to correct them.

`rhythm.lyric_adjacent_prose`

## The Revision Pass

### The Length-Variation Audit

**Also called:** the word-count column, the sentence-length series, the numbers pass
**What it is:** A mechanical check: number every sentence on a page by word count, write the series down the margin, and read the numbers instead of the prose.
**Effect on the audience:** None directly. It is a measuring instrument, and it catches the one fault your ear consistently misses, because your ear supplies the variety your sentences lack.
**Used for and where it works best:** Do it on one page per chapter and on every opening and closing page. You want range and irregularity — something like 6, 18, 11, 3, 24, 9 — and no run of four consecutive sentences within about three words of each other. The craft rule is to fix the flattest run first and leave the rest alone: correcting every number produces `rhythm.audible_technique` from the other direction, a page engineered into deliberate zigzag. Do the same count on sentences per paragraph (`rhythm.paragraph_breath`). This is the diagnostic for `rhythm.monotone_length` and the tuning of `rhythm.length_as_tempo`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Essay, Short Story, Memoir, Voiceover Script | genres: all
**Avoid when:** You are drafting. Counting words while generating them stops the generating, and the numbers are meaningless before the structure is fixed.
**Example:**
> Before: 14, 16, 13, 15, 12, 17, 14 — a flat page, nothing technically wrong with it, and the reader will skim it.
>
> After: 14, 16, 4, 27, 12, 3, 14 — same content, two sentences merged and two split, and the page now has a pulse.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.first_draft_cadence` — while you are still drafting. Counting words while generating them stops the generating, and the numbers are meaningless before the structure is fixed; decide the cadence in advance instead.  
`rhythm.length_audit`

---

### Hearing Your Own Tics

**Also called:** the frequency pass, crutch words, private verbal habits
**What it is:** Finding the words and shapes you reach for unconsciously, by counting rather than by remembering, and then hunting those specific items rather than following general advice.
**Effect on the audience:** Invisible when fixed; corrosive when not. A reader who has met your favourite construction eleven times in a chapter starts noticing you instead of the scene, and cannot say why.
**Used for and where it works best:** Run a word-frequency count over five thousand words of your own finished prose and read the top fifty entries after the function words. That list — not anyone else's list — is your search-and-destroy set for the rest of your career. The craft rule is that tics are structural as well as lexical: the habitual dash, the habitual three-item list, the habitual short sentence after the long one, the habitual paragraph that ends on a one-line beat. Count those too, by hand, over ten pages. See `rhythm.audible_technique` and `voice.voice_bible`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Essay, Memoir, Short Story, Podcast | genres: all
**Avoid when:** You purge a word that is doing real work. Some repetition is voice and some is a motif (`theme.thematic_motif`); the test is whether you chose it, not whether it recurs.
**Example:**
> Frequency count on a finished chapter, function words removed: *just* (31), *something* (24), *a kind of* (19), *and then* (17), *slightly* (15).
>
> Nothing on that list is a bad word. All five together are a fingerprint, and four of them are hedges — which means the chapter is not describing, it is approximating.

**Yields to:** `theme.thematic_motif` — wherever you are about to purge a word that is doing real work. Some repetition is voice and some is a motif; the test is whether you chose it, not whether it recurs.  
`rhythm.tic_audit`

---

### The First-Draft Cadence Trap

**Also called:** your resting rhythm, the default music, writing in your own key
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Every writer has a cadence a first draft falls into unsupervised. The trap is mistaking that cadence for the voice of the piece, and then defending it in revision precisely because it sounds like you.
**Effect on the audience:** Across one piece, nothing obvious. Across a body of work, every narrator sounds the same, every register is the same distance from the reader, and readers who liked the first book find the third familiar in a way they cannot name and do not enjoy.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, as an unexamined default. On a briefed piece, choose a provisional cadence before drafting: write one paragraph deliberately in a rhythm that is not yours — longer, flatter, more coordinated, more clipped — and keep it beside you as a tuning fork. On a genuinely exploratory draft, do not freeze that test into the final register; discover the best page first, then let `voice.register_setting` set the formality band on the second pass. In both cases audit the draft against evidence rather than against the ear that produced the default. See `voice.sentence_rhythm`, `voice.narrator_vs_character`, `rhythm.tic_audit`.
**Example:**
> Draft opening of a novel about a nineteen-year-old conscript: "The morning was cold, and there was that particular quality of light that comes just before the year turns, when everything looks slightly further away than it is."
>
> That is a forty-year-old essayist's cadence, and it will be the cadence of all four hundred pages unless it is caught here. The conscript's: "It was cold. It was always cold by then. You stopped saying it after the first week because nobody answered."

**Yields to:** `voice.sentence_rhythm` — always, as an unexamined default. Write one paragraph deliberately in a rhythm that is not yours and keep it beside you as a tuning fork, then audit against that rather than against the ear that produced the problem.  
`rhythm.first_draft_cadence`
