## More Named Failures

### Every Sentence Starts the Same Way

**Also called:** the subject-verb file, the opening-word rut, the participial parade
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A page on which nearly every sentence opens the same way — subject then verb, or the same pronoun nine times, or a run of participial openings ("Walking to the door, she...", "Reaching for the light, she...").
**Effect on the audience:** The reader stops hearing individual sentences and starts processing a texture. Attention survives about four repetitions; after that the page is being scanned, not read.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, except as a deliberate short run — a stretch of identical openings can render obsession or drill, and `rhythm.anaphora` is exactly this fault done on purpose and stopped in time. The diagnostic is mechanical: copy the first three words of every sentence on a page into a column and read the column. The fix is not to invent inversions; it is to front an adverbial on one sentence in five (`rhythm.withheld_subject`) and to merge two sentences into one where the second is really a continuation.
**Example:**
> Before: "She checked the ledger. She found the entry for March. She read it twice. She closed the book. She went to find him."
>
> After: "She checked the ledger. March was there, in the same hand as the rest, and she read it twice before she was sure. Then she closed the book and went to find him."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.anaphora` for the deliberate version — this fault done on purpose and stopped in time — and `rhythm.withheld_subject` for the repair, which is to front an adverbial on one sentence in five rather than to invent inversions.  
`rhythm.same_sentence_opener`

---

### The Relentless Fragment

**Also called:** the all-fragment voice, staccato disease, permanent emphasis
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Prose in which most sentences are fragments — no subject, no verb, punctuated for impact — sustained for pages rather than deployed in beats.
**Effect on the audience:** Intensity everywhere, which is intensity nowhere. Worse, the prose loses the ability to be fast, because speed is relative and there is nothing slow left to be fast against.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always past about three in a row. A fragment works by leaning on a complete sentence next to it, which supplies the words it left out — remove every complete sentence and the fragments have nothing to lean on and start reading as notes. The fix: keep the best one in each run of four and restore the others to full sentences, then check that the survivors still fall where something changes. See `rhythm.fragment` for the working version.
**Example:**
> Before: "The corridor. Dark. Longer than he remembered. A door at the end. Locked, probably. No sound. Nothing. Just the hum of something behind the wall. Waiting."
>
> After: "The corridor was longer than he remembered, and dark all the way to the door at the end. Locked, probably. Behind the wall something hummed, and went on humming, and did not stop."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.fragment` — always past about three in a row. A fragment works by leaning on a complete sentence next to it; remove every complete sentence and the fragments have nothing to lean on and start reading as notes.  
`rhythm.fragment_voice`

---

### Rhythm Borrowed From a Writer You Admire

**Also called:** the ventriloquised cadence, undeclared pastiche, the influence hangover
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Taking a writer's surface rhythm wholesale — their sentence length, their conjunctions, their punctuation habits — and applying it to material that has nothing to do with theirs.
**Effect on the audience:** Split. The reader who knows the source hears the source and stops reading you. The reader who does not hears a voice at odds with the subject and cannot locate the discomfort, which is worse, because it registers as the writing being somehow untrue.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, once past apprenticeship — and note that declared pastiche is a different thing entirely, legitimate in comedy, in historical register and in heritage work where the borrowed cadence is the point. The fix is to take the structural lesson and change the surface: if what you actually admire is that they withhold the verb, keep the withholding and write it in your own sentence lengths. Compare `rhythm.first_draft_cadence`, the same problem with yourself as the model, and `voice.tonal_drift`.
**Example:**
> Borrowed: "And he rode out and the country was wide before him and there was no road and no water and he did not stop." (A Baghdad procurement scandal does not want a Cormac McCarthy sentence.)
>
> Own: "He drove out at four with no route and half a tank, because the road to the site had not officially existed since 2014."

**Yields to:** `voice.pastiche_vs_parody` — Declared pastiche; the borrowed cadence is the point.  
`rhythm.borrowed_rhythm`

---

### Comma Splices Used Without Intent

**Also called:** the accidental run-on, unlicensed splicing, the typo that isn't
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Two independent clauses joined by a comma with no rhythmic purpose — not for speed, not for interior voice, just because the writer did not decide what the sentence was doing.
**Effect on the audience:** It reads as a typographical error, and the cost is not local: a reader who has decided you do not control your punctuation discounts every deliberate effect that follows, including the splices you meant.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, and the test is one question — can you say what this splice does that a full stop would not? If the answer is "it flows better", it is a mistake. Intentional splicing needs short, closely linked clauses and otherwise impeccable prose around it to signal the licence; see `rhythm.comma_splice_tool`. In reportage, legal and corporate copy there is no licence available at all.
**Example:**
> Unintentional: "The committee met on the Thursday, the report had been circulated the previous week, most members had not read it, this was mentioned by nobody."
>
> Fixed: "The committee met on the Thursday. The report had been circulated the previous week and most members had not read it. Nobody mentioned this."
>
> Intentional, in a different register: "She didn't answer, she didn't move, she just let the phone ring out on the table between them."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.comma_splice_tool` — always, and the test is one question: can you say what this splice does that a full stop would not? If the answer is "it flows better", it is a mistake.  
`rhythm.unintended_splice`

---

### The Sentence That Scans Well and Means Nothing

**Also called:** empty music, the beautiful nothing, cadence without content
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A sentence whose rhythm is perfect — balanced limbs, ending on a stress, eminently quotable — and whose content is a tautology, a cliché, or a claim that could not be false.
**Effect on the audience:** Momentary admiration, then a small withdrawal of trust that the reader cannot account for. They have registered that nothing was said in a sentence that behaved as though something was.
**Used for and where it works best:** formats: — | genres: —
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always — and it is the hardest failure to cut, because it passes every rhythm test in Part 1 and usually feels like the best sentence on the page. The diagnostic: rewrite it as flatly as you can, in the plainest words available, and ask whether the flat version is worth saying. If it is not, the music was carrying an empty box. It is the twin of `rhythm.overwritten_sentence` — that one has too much ornament for its content, this one has no content at all — and it is where `theme.explained_theme` usually enters a manuscript.
**Example:**
> Before: "In the end, the past is never past, and what we carry long enough, we become."
>
> After: "He kept his father's toolbox for thirty years and never once opened it."

**Yields to:** `rhythm.concrete_nouns` — The music carries no content; name the object.  
`rhythm.empty_music`

- Verse and lyric-adjacent prose — 1 card (`lyric_adjacent_prose`)
- The revision pass — 3 cards (`length_audit`, `tic_audit`, `first_draft_cadence`)
- More named failures — 5 cards (`same_sentence_opener`, `fragment_voice`, `borrowed_rhythm`, `unintended_splice`, `empty_music`)

Seven of the 41 are defect cards: `translationese_scan`, `first_draft_cadence`, `same_sentence_opener`, `fragment_voice`, `borrowed_rhythm`, `unintended_splice`, `empty_music`.

Highest value first — rhythm in headlines, decks and standfirsts; first-person against third-person rhythm and the way close third borrows a character's sentence length; present-tense rhythm and why it resists the long sentence. Then: comic timing at sentence level as a rhythm problem rather than a joke-construction one; pace across a serialised release and what the gap between episodes does to a chapter ending; typography, measure and line length as pacing, and mobile reading against print; rhythm in email and chat register; assonance and vowel colour; repeating a single word across a page as a structural device; the callback line's rhythm; scene-and-sequel alternation heard as pace; read-aloud rhythm for picture books and children's writing. Remaining named failures: the stacked prepositional phrase, the buried verb, throat-clearing openings, the comma-comma-comma sentence, over-punctuation, the false-profound short paragraph, and accidental sing-song metre.
